description: Versioned machine-readable contract for the Harvest management API. Update this file and CHANGELOG.md whenever a route is added, removed, renamed, or its request/response shape changes.

breaking_changes: Changing the type of a response field
Renaming a route (path or method change)
Changing a query parameter from optional to required
Adding a new mutating route without classifying it in this contract
non_breaking_changes: Adding a new optional response field
Adding a new optional query parameter
Adding a new optional request body field
Narrowing an existing error response to be more specific
compatibility.conditional_shape_note: Issue #756 partial-availability carve-out to "Changing the type of a response field": the cross-shard list read endpoints GET /workflows (non-paginated), GET /workers, GET /admin/schedules, GET /dead-letters, and GET /dags return a CONDITIONAL 200 shape — a bare JSON array when every expected shard is reachable (status == complete), or a degraded object { "<items>": [...], "status": "partial"|"unavailable", "unavailable_shards": [{ "shard_id", "reason" }] } when a shard is unavailable. This is NOT a breaking change to any currently-successful response: the all-reachable array is byte-for-byte identical to the pre-#756 shape, and the object form only replaces what was previously a whole-request 500 (a failed, non-successful response), so no client that received a successful response before can observe a changed type. The paginated GET /workflows object shape and the aggregate/health object endpoints (GET /dead-letters/aggregate, GET /workers/health) instead gain status/unavailable_shards as always-present ADDITIVE fields (a non-breaking change).

auth_note: Route authorization posture is classified in issue #174. This contract records the route surface and category; auth enforcement is separate.
audit_note: Mutating routes (read_only: false) are covered by the audit trail (issue #158). The audit endpoint itself is read-only.
openapi_note: Two OpenAPI 3.1 documents are generated from this file (issue #694): autumn-harvest-plugin/openapi.json, which the crate compiles in and serves, and docs/openapi.json, the pretty-printed copy. Run `scripts/regenerate-openapi.sh` whenever a route, parameter, request field or response field changes here; it writes both. Every parameter must declare `in` and `required`, and every request body must declare `required`. The transform rejects an entry that does not, and refuses a request body on a read method. See docs/openapi.md.

routes.description: List workflow executions with optional filters. Supports keyset cursor pagination (issue #498). A malformed percent-encoded query-string byte sequence (an invalid UTF-8 byte, or an incomplete/non-hex `%` escape) is rejected with a 400 before any parameter is parsed, rather than silently substituting the Unicode replacement character and proceeding with a wrong-but-plausible value (issue #1151, sweeping the issue #774 `queue-coverage` fix to every other raw-pairs route).

params.name: state
params.description: Comma-separated execution states (e.g. RUNNING,FAILED).

params.name: workflow_name
params.description: Filter by registered workflow name.

params.name: owner
params.description: Filter by the execution owner, matched exactly. A blank value is ignored.

params.name: severity
params.description: Filter by the execution severity label, matched exactly. A blank value is ignored.

params.name: search_attr
params.description: Search attribute filter in key:value form (exact-match string equality). May be repeated.

params.name: search_attr_filter
params.description: Typed comparison/set predicate over search attributes in key:op:value form, op in {eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte, in, exists} (issue #506). Repeatable; ANDed. Numeric values compare numerically, booleans as booleans, else strings. Comparison ops require a numeric value. Malformed predicates and nested .-paths return 400. Backed by the existing idx_harvest_we_search GIN index (no migration).

params.name: limit
params.description: Maximum number of results to return (legacy; use page_size for paginated access).

params.name: page_size
params.description: Number of results per page (1–200). Activates the paginated response envelope {workflows, next_cursor}.

params.name: cursor
params.description: Opaque keyset pagination cursor from a previous response's next_cursor field.

params.name: order
params.description: Sort direction: 'asc' (oldest first) or 'desc' (newest first, default). Activates the paginated response envelope.

params.name: started_after
params.description: Filter to executions whose started_at is after this RFC 3339 timestamp (e.g. 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z).

params.name: started_before
params.description: Filter to executions whose started_at is before this RFC 3339 timestamp.

params.name: exec_id_prefix
params.description: Case-insensitive prefix match on the execution UUID string.

params.name: sla_breached
params.description: When 'true', return only executions whose soft SLA has been breached (issue #487).

params.name: nd_blocked
params.description: When 'true', return only RUNNING executions currently blocked on replay non-determinism (issue #603). Each row carries nd_blocked_at / nd_block_reason / nd_block_count plus the structured divergence diagnostic (failure_cause, expected, actual, event_index, workflow_type, build_id) in search_attrs.

params.name: legal_hold
params.description: When 'true', return only executions currently under an active legal hold (issue #747): legal_hold_set_at IS NOT NULL AND (legal_hold_until IS NULL OR legal_hold_until > now).

params.name: start_source
params.description: Filter by workflow-start provenance (issue #740). One of the bounded StartSource set: api, schedule, backfill, signal_with_start, update_with_start, completion_trigger, webhook, child, batch, continue_as_new, reset, outbox, or 'unknown' (matches NULL / pre-upgrade rows). Any other value returns 400.

params.name: failure_cause
params.description: Filter to executions whose search_attrs carry this failure_cause value.

params.name: no_progress_minutes
params.description: Stalled-workflow discovery (issue #486). A positive integer N. Returns RUNNING and SUSPENDED executions with no recorded progress for N minutes, sorted by staleness. PAUSED executions are excluded unless state=PAUSED is given, because a pause blocks progress by design. Keyset pagination does not apply on this path. A value below 1, or a non-numeric value, returns 400. Cannot be combined with history_bloat_min_events, which returns 400.

params.name: include_sleeping
params.description: When 'true', keep correctly-sleeping executions in the no_progress_minutes result. An execution is correctly sleeping when a future-dated timer is its only pending item and no timer is overdue. Such an execution is excluded by default, because it has nothing to progress on.

params.name: min_history_events
params.description: General-purpose history-size filter (issue #493). A non-negative integer N. Restricts the response to executions whose recorded harvest_events count is >= N. Composes freely with state, order and pagination, unlike history_bloat_min_events.

params.name: history_bloat_min_events
params.description: Operator early-warning discovery for workflow history bloat (issue #704). A non-negative integer N. Restricts the response to live (non-terminal) executions whose current recorded harvest_events count is >= N, sorted by history size descending (largest first), each row carrying its history_event_count so callers can rank/triage without a second call. Not supported together with cursor/page_size/order pagination (results are sorted by a computed value, which has no keyset cursor) -- combining them returns 400. A non-numeric or negative value returns 400. Deliberately a DIFFERENT query parameter from the unrelated, pre-existing general-purpose min_history_events filter (issue #493), which composes freely with state=/order=/pagination and returns executions of any state in the caller's chosen order -- the two parameters must never be conflated (see PR #1139 review).

success_response.description: Without pagination params: bare JSON array of execution objects on the happy path (backward compatible); on shard degradation the { workflows, status, unavailable_shards } envelope (see below). With cursor/page_size/order: JSON object {"workflows": [...], "next_cursor": <string|null>, "status": "complete"|"partial"|"unavailable", "unavailable_shards": [{ "shard_id", "reason" }]} — for the paginated object shape, status and unavailable_shards are ALWAYS present (additive fields; status is "complete" and unavailable_shards is [] on the happy path). Partial availability (issue #756): when a shard is unreachable this endpoint returns 200 with the union of reachable-shard results (the non-paginated bare array degrades to the same { workflows, status, unavailable_shards } object) instead of failing the whole request with a 500; an unreachable shard is named in unavailable_shards rather than being silently dropped. On the happy path (all shards reachable) the non-paginated response shape is byte-for-byte unchanged. With history_bloat_min_events set (issue #704): each returned row additionally carries history_event_count (an integer, omitted on every other request); rows are always non-terminal and sorted by history_event_count descending regardless of any order= param (which is rejected when combined -- see the history_bloat_min_events param description). The unrelated pre-existing min_history_events filter (issue #493) composes with state=/order=/pagination normally and does not affect sort order or add history_event_count to the response.

error_responses.description: Invalid filter value, bad RFC 3339 timestamp, unknown order direction, or history_bloat_min_events combined with cursor/page_size/order pagination.

routes.description: Recursive cross-shard execution lineage tree (issue #621): the full descendant tree rooted at {id}, so an operator triaging a DLQ/stuck alert can locate the failed descendant of a multi-level saga in ONE call instead of hand-walking parent_id links level by level and shard by shard. Rooting at a mid-tree node returns just the subtree below it; the chosen root is always depth 0 and still reports its own parent_id. Each node carries execution_id, workflow_name, workflow_id, state, started_at, closed_at, parent_id, depth, shard_id, and the spawn relationship (await_mode `awaited`/`detached` plus parent_close_policy when detached); children is always an array, empty for a leaf (never an error). The walk fans out across every readable shard (the iter_shards() aggregation pattern), so a child placed on a different shard than its parent by rendezvous hashing still appears. Recursion is bounded by max_depth (default 20, ceiling 50) and max_nodes (default 1000, ceiling 10000, counted INCLUDING the root); hitting either sets truncated=true with a machine-readable truncation_reason (`max_depth` | `max_nodes`) and names the dropped subtrees' parents in truncated_parent_ids (bounded, with truncated_parents_capped when it overflowed) — never a silent cap. Only parents that PROVABLY have children are named (via a bounded existence probe), so an operator is never sent chasing a subtree that does not exist. A visited-set guarantees each execution_id appears exactly once and a malformed parent_id loop terminates instead of recursing. `?summary=true` returns the per-state DESCENDANT roll-up (counts keyed by lowercased state, every known state always present even at 0; the root's own state is echoed on `root` and excluded from counts) plus total_descendants, for an at-a-glance health check without transferring the tree. Cross-shard degradation (issue #756): an unreachable shard is named in unavailable_shards with status `partial`/`unavailable` rather than failing the whole call — a triage read must not 500 during the incident it exists to diagnose. NOT admin-gated, matching GET /workflows/{id}/children (which already traverses depth cross-shard over the same rows). SNAPSHOT CONSISTENCY: shards are read independently, so a tree may be marginally time-skewed across shards; acceptable for triage. Adds no WorkflowEvent variant, no migration, appends no events, performs no writes. A malformed percent-encoded query-string byte sequence (an invalid UTF-8 byte, or an incomplete/non-hex `%` escape) is rejected with a 400 before any parameter is parsed, rather than silently substituting the Unicode replacement character and proceeding with a wrong-but-plausible value (issue #1151, sweeping the issue #774 `queue-coverage` fix to every other raw-pairs route).

params.name: id
params.description: Root execution UUID (may be any node in the tree).

params.name: max_depth
params.description: Recursion depth cap below the root. Default 20, must be 1–50. Out of range is rejected with 400 rather than silently clamped.

params.name: max_nodes
params.description: Total node cap INCLUDING the root. Default 1000, must be 1–10000. Out of range is rejected with 400.

params.name: summary
params.description: `true`/`1` returns the per-state descendant roll-up instead of the nested tree.

success_response.notes: The body is POLYMORPHIC. Default (tree) mode returns root (a nested node whose `children` array recurses), node_count, and max_depth_reached. `?summary=true` returns root as a compact {execution_id, workflow_name, workflow_id, state} ref plus counts (map of lowercased state -> descendant count) and total_descendants, and omits node_count/children. Both shapes carry truncated, truncation_reason (omitted when null), truncated_parent_ids, truncated_parents_capped, limits (the bounds actually applied), status, and unavailable_shards. The fields list above is the UNION of both shapes. retained_summary_parent_ids (issue #752) names nodes in the returned tree that have at least one child DEMOTED INTO A RETENTION SUMMARY and therefore omitted from the tree along with everything beneath it; it is empty unless tiered summary retention is enabled. It is a THIRD, independent incompleteness signal: truncated=false AND status=complete together still do not mean every descendant is present -- check this list too. The omitted rows remain readable via GET /workflows/summaries.

error_responses.description: Malformed execution ID, or an out-of-range/non-numeric max_depth or max_nodes (the message names the offending bound).

Root execution not found. Also returned when the id encodes a shard neither this node's pools nor the router know about (nothing here could host it), and for a classic DAG run, which is not on the execution path.

The root's own shard could not be queried, so existence is undetermined (retriable): the id encodes a shard this deployment knows about (router-readable or default) but which has no configured storage pool on this node — the normal state mid a shard-add rollout — or that shard's pool connection could not be acquired. Deliberately not a 404: answering 'not found' would be a false negative for a run that may exist on its own shard. Note this applies only to the ROOT lookup; an unreachable shard encountered during the DESCENDANT walk degrades to 200 with status=partial and the shard named in unavailable_shards.

success_response.notes: Each entry in pending_activities and pending_local_activities carries an optional nested last_failure object (issue #773) — {error_type, error, attempt, non_retryable, failed_at?, details?} — omitted entirely when the activity has never failed, so healthy-run responses stay byte-identical to pre-#773 builds. It answers "why is this activity retrying?" alongside the next_retry_at countdown without a second round-trip. Availability of the fields differs by activity kind because retryable failures are not event-sourced (an AC2-vs-AC5 reconciliation; #773 adds no migration): for a backing-off REGULAR (task-queue) activity — the primary case — last_failure is sourced from the harvest_task_queue.error column that queue::requeue_for_retry sets on each retryable failure (no ActivityFailed event is appended), so error and attempt are present, error_type defaults to "Error", non_retryable is false, and failed_at/details are omitted (the task row has no failure timestamp or structured detail); for LOCAL activities (and any event-sourced failure) last_failure is sourced from the most recent LocalActivityFailed event and includes failed_at (the event timestamp), with error_type "Error", non_retryable false, and no details. When read-path payload decoding (issue #608) is active for the request, last_failure.error is tolerantly decoded like every other payload field.

routes.description: Reconstruct a single execution's timeline (per-step durations, busy-vs-wait split, slowest step) purely from recorded history; no new events are appended and no state is recomputed. Surfaces only durations, names, ids, and outcomes — never any input/output/payload/error/value field — so read-path payload decoding (issue #608) is a no-op and is skipped. Classic DAG runs are not on the execution path and return 404; unified DAG runs lower onto the standard execution path and return 200 like any workflow execution. The wait_ms/exec_ms split is present ONLY for regular activity steps that recorded a claim/start timestamp; it is null for child_workflow, local_activity, external activities (issue #92 — these render as activity steps with no split), timer, signal_wait, side_effect, and for activities with no recorded start. total_ms is always present. Rollup attribution: a started activity's queue-wait split goes to rollup.wait_ms and its exec split to rollup.busy_ms; a regular activity (one reporting an attempt) with a null split never started (pending or a schedule-to-start timeout) so its whole total_ms is queue-wait and goes to rollup.wait_ms; external activities, child_workflow, local_activity, and side_effect totals go to rollup.busy_ms; timer and signal_wait totals go to rollup.wait_ms. For a retried activity, wait_ms spans all prior attempts' execution and backoff, not only queue wait — treat it as an upper bound on queue wait. Known limitation: the full event history is loaded with no LIMIT (bounded by workflow continue-as-new discipline, the ≤500-event target), so a run with a very large history makes this read proportionally expensive.

routes.description: Durable per-execution author log lines (issue #790): the lines a workflow emitted through ctx.logger()/ctx.log_info/log_warn/log_error, persisted to harvest_workflow_logs when the opt-in durable sink is enabled via HarvestBuilder::workflow_log_persistence. Admin-gated: a log message is free-form author text that routinely carries business detail, so this read takes the stricter posture of the sibling per-execution diagnostics (/awaitables) rather than the plain execution-row one. Lines are returned in EMISSION order (the deterministic seq logical-position key), never occurred_at, which is wall clock and can be non-monotonic across workers; seq is also the pagination cursor. Each element of lines[] carries seq (i64), level (info|warn|error), message (string, capped at write time), occurred_at (RFC 3339), and truncation_marker (bool, present only when true). When an execution exceeds its configured per-execution line cap, the newest lines are dropped and a single synthetic marker row is appended (drop-newest); the response-level truncated flag is filter-independent, so a ?level=error page still reports it. Logs are OBSERVATIONAL ONLY: they are not part of the event history, carry no determinism guarantee, and are never read back into workflow logic. With the sink disabled this endpoint returns an empty lines[] for every execution. Log rows are removed by the same ON DELETE CASCADE that removes the execution, so they can never outlive workflow-history retention, and targeted PII erasure (issue #495) deletes them too. Shard routing fails closed (no default-shard fallback): an empty list is a legitimate answer for a run that never logged, so a mis-routed read would be indistinguishable from "no logs" and returns 503 instead. A malformed percent-encoded query-string byte sequence (an invalid UTF-8 byte, or an incomplete/non-hex `%` escape) is rejected with a 400 before any parameter is parsed, rather than silently substituting the Unicode replacement character and proceeding with a wrong-but-plausible value (issue #1151, sweeping the issue #774 `queue-coverage` fix to every other raw-pairs route).

params.description: Page size; default 200. Values above 1000 are clamped down; a value <= 0 is rejected with 400 rather than clamped up.

params.description: Exclusive keyset cursor: the previous page's last seq. `after` is accepted as an alias.

params.name: level
params.description: Repeatable, or comma-separated. One of info, warn, error. An unknown value returns 400 rather than silently matching nothing — a typo would otherwise answer "no lines" for a run that has plenty. Omitted means all levels.

routes.description: Per-execution stall diagnosis (issue #809): answers "is this run healthily waiting or pathologically stuck, and what is the actionable root cause?" in one call, replacing the 4+ endpoint correlation an operator does by hand today. Returns a one-word triage `health` (`healthy` | `stalled` | `degraded` | `blocked_external` | `terminal`), a discriminated `blocked_on` object, and `last_event_age_seconds`. `blocked_on` is internally tagged on `type` (snake_case) and closed over: `healthy_in_progress`; `awaiting_signal` {signal_name, since?}; `sleeping_timer` {fires_at}; `pending_child` {child_exec_id, child_state}; `activity_retrying` {activity_name, attempt, last_error?, next_attempt_at?}; `activity_deferred` {activity_name?, next_attempt_at}; `activity_no_worker` {queue, activity_name?}; `activity_circuit_open` {activity_name, phase, forced_open, cooldown_until?} (`phase` is `open` | `half_open`: a half-open breaker admits a probe right now and closes on success, so its `health` is `healthy` (and `forced_open` is always `false`, since a forced-open breaker's phase never leaves `open` until an explicit force-close); an `open` breaker with `forced_open: false` was tripped organically and self-heals on its own cooldown timer with no operator action, but issue #369's non-retryable `ActivityFailure::circuit_open` fast-fails every dispatch until then -- the activity is heading for a terminal failure, not progress, so its `health` is `degraded`, not `healthy` and not `stalled`; an `open` breaker with `forced_open: true` was operator-forced -- no probe is admitted on any timer -- and needs an explicit force-close, so its `health` is `stalled` (issue #1193). `forced_open` is the AUTHORITATIVE discriminator, sourced directly from the in-process registry's own flag -- NOT inferred from whether `cooldown_until` is present (issue #1193 Codex round-1 P2 on PR #1365): a policy cooldown configured outside `chrono`'s representable range makes an organically-tripped breaker ALSO report `cooldown_until` absent, which would be indistinguishable from a forced-open one by that field alone; `cooldown_until` remains present only as an informational display deadline when it can be computed. An organic trip whose `cooldown_until` is at or before the row's own EFFECTIVE dispatch instant (`max(now, scheduled_at)` -- `now` for an already-due row, since it could be attempted any moment) does NOT report `activity_circuit_open` at all (issue #1193 Codex round-4/round-5 P2): `CircuitBreakerRegistry::on_dispatch` checks the elapsed cooldown at the actual dispatch instant, so this row's own future attempt is what would be admitted as the recovery probe rather than fast-failed, and the row instead reports the ordinary `activity_retrying` / `activity_deferred` (or, for an already-due, otherwise-unimpeded row, `healthy_in_progress`) it would without a breaker in the way. A forced-open breaker has no cooldown to compare against and is unaffected by this exception. The comparison uses a wall-clock timestamp captured back-to-back with the breaker snapshot read, not the (potentially much earlier, pre-database-query) `now` the rest of the diagnosis is timestamped with, so the derived `cooldown_until` does not systematically underestimate the true deadline. In a fan-out containing any two of the three circuit shapes, the more severe one outranks the less severe one in the precedence ladder below (forced-open > organic-open > half-open), so the genuinely actionable stall is never masked by a self-healing or already-recovering one purely because of row order -- forced vs organic was Codex round-1 P1 on PR #1365, organic vs half-open was Codex round-2 P1 on the same PR: the two used to share a tier while also sharing a health value, so a tie was harmless until `Degraded` split them apart); `activity_rate_limited` {key, activity_name?}; `activity_rate_limit_bucket_missing` {key, activity_name?} (the bucket row does not exist, so the claim gate's `EXISTS` refuses it forever -- `stalled`, unlike the refilling `activity_rate_limited`); `activity_concurrency_deferred` {key, activity_name?}; `activity_queue_paused` {queue, activity_name?}; `activity_paused` {activity_name} (an operator paused the activity TYPE (#807), so claim_task's paused_activities anti-join holds it on every queue on the shard -- distinct from the queue-wide activity_queue_paused, and ranked just under it because the queue pause is the broader lever); `awaiting_external_handoff` {token, activity_name?}; `paused` {actor?, since?}; `non_determinism_blocked` {since, reason?, block_count}; `awaiting_replay_wait` {wait_kind, name?, since?}; `workflow_no_worker` {queue}; `workflow_queue_paused` {queue}; `timer_overdue{fires_at,overdue_by_seconds}`, `no_pending_work`. Optional members are omitted, never null. Correlates, in a single shard-local read: the pending stack, per-queue worker liveness (the canonical #774 worker_covers_queue predicate, so it cannot drift from /admin/queue-coverage) -- a PENDING row asks whether any worker can claim it right now (Active only, since a Draining worker claims nothing new), while a HELD row asks whether its own recorded claimant is still alive (Active OR Draining, because a worker that has begun a graceful shutdown still runs its held work to completion) plus the row's own claim gates -- required build (#171/#604), required capabilities (#804) and session pin (#606), each evaluated against the SAME worker; an activity row with NO required_capabilities snapshot (a legacy or manual enqueue) is still gated by its REGISTERED handler's requires, mirroring claim_task's ineligible-activities gate, so an un-snapshotted row no worker can claim is reported as a stall rather than as healthy progress, the in-process circuit registry (#369, consulted via list() only -- never on_dispatch/force_* -- so diagnosing can never advance a breaker's phase; and because that registry is per worker PROCESS, its phase is reported only when this API replica's own co-located worker is the SOLE worker that could claim the row, since a peer replica whose breaker is closed can still dispatch it -- a fleet-wide outage is therefore deliberately under-reported rather than risking a false stall, and /admin/circuits per replica remains the authoritative per-breaker surface), rate-limit bucket and per-key concurrency saturation (shaped exactly like claim_task's own gates; a circuit-breaker-tracked activity's bucket is never itself the claim-time impediment regardless of build, since the breaker gates it at dispatch instead (#369) -- but THIS replica's tracked/untracked fact about an activity is an in-process compile-time declaration, and whether it can be trusted for a given row is build-scoped (#1190): both activity_rate_limited and activity_rate_limit_bucket_missing are reported only when every worker eligible to claim the row shares this replica's build, so during a rolling deploy an eligible peer on a different build -- which may declare the breaker differently in EITHER direction, tracked here but not there or vice versa -- never has a rate-limit verdict fabricated for it, the same unknown-worker-is-assumed-capable rule the circuit registry follows above), the operator queue-pause table (#619), and the task row's own attempt/error/scheduled_at retry timing. Every activity row is classified and the WORST by a fixed cross-task precedence ladder wins (queue_paused, then activity_paused, no_worker, rate_limit_bucket_missing, circuit_open[forced_open: true], circuit_open[forced_open: false, phase: open], circuit_open[phase: half_open], concurrency_deferred, rate_limited, retrying, deferred, healthy), so one wedged slot in a wide fan-out is never masked by a milder sibling -- including a forced-open breaker never being masked by an organically-tripped one (issue #1193 Codex round-1 P1) and an organically-tripped breaker never being masked by a half-open one (issue #1193 Codex round-2 P1) at a different activity in the same fan-out. ONE exception to "the activity bucket always wins over the workflow task" (issue #1193 Codex round-3 P1): when the winning activity verdict resolves to health degraded specifically, and the run's OWN workflow task cannot be claimed at all (workflow_no_worker or workflow_queue_paused), THAT is reported instead -- a frozen decision cycle is worse than one activity self-resolving into a failure, and unlike every other activity health this one carries no such guarantee on its own. Every other activity health (stalled, blocked_external, healthy) keeps the pre-existing, deliberately-activity-first behavior unchanged. Within a single row the three non-self-healing gates (queue_paused, no_worker, circuit_open) are checked first, then the not-yet-due branch, then the two self-healing gates: a task that is not yet due has not reached the claim gates at all, so reporting a momentarily-saturated bucket would drop the attempt/last_error/next_attempt_at an operator needs. A future scheduled_at alone does NOT mean failed-and-retrying -- the dispatcher also pushes a task forward with no failure at all (dispatch-time rate-limit deferral, which even decrements the claim-time attempt back down, plus session-capacity and capability-miss redelivery), so the not-yet-due branch reports activity_retrying only when there is failure evidence (a recorded error, which a later deferral never clears) and activity_deferred otherwise. A claimed (RUNNING) row is healthy only while a live worker still polls its queue -- a claimed row whose fleet is gone is a poison-pill orphan (#367), not progress. health is derived from the verdict class alone and never from event age, so a long durable sleep reports healthy no matter how old its last event is. contributing_reason_codes is the UNION of every claim-time impediment across ALL of the execution's activity rows -- not just the row blocked_on names -- so a lower-ranked cause is never hidden behind a higher-ranked sibling in a fan-out; it is sourced verbatim from the eligibility explainer's own pure task_intrinsic_impediment_reasons (#611) so the single-verdict and multi-reason surfaces cannot drift in how a cause is named. Worker liveness is the one reason that is NOT a claim-time gate, so it is reported for a HELD row too -- but keyed on the same question the verdict asks: a PENDING row on claim eligibility (an Active worker could claim it), a HELD row on its own recorded claimant's liveness (Active OR Draining). Without that split the codes contradict the verdict in both directions -- a row held by a live draining claimant would report healthy yet carry no_live_worker, and an orphan held by a dead claimant would OMIT it whenever a live Active peer happens to cover the queue. An awaited-but-unsent signal is visible only to the #615 replay drive, which is comparatively expensive and ranks below activities/handoffs/children, so it is consulted ONLY when the database-observable categories would otherwise resolve to sleeping_timer or no_pending_work -- wait_set reports replayed, history_only (with wait_set_reason: an upstream reason such as handler_not_registered passed through verbatim, else wait_set_unavailable when the replay errors, wait_set_timed_out when it exceeds the query timeout, or execution_went_terminal on a TOCTOU race) or not_consulted accordingly; the replay is bounded by the server's query timeout; the verdict is identical either way and the common wedged-activity path never pays for a replay. Every OTHER awaitable kind replay can name -- a command-less ctx.await_condition park, a durable mutex acquire (#691), an admitted update awaiting its handler, a parked external-workflow operation (#492/#757/#751) -- leaves no row in any side table this endpoint reads, so replay is the only source that can see it; those report awaiting_replay_wait (blocked_external) naming the kind. They are consulted BELOW every side-table cause, so they can only ever replace what would otherwise be a false no_pending_work and can never mask a more precise verdict such as sleeping_timer. Below every category above sits the run's OWN workflow task row (task_type = 'workflow'), consulted purely as a fallback so it can never mask a real cause: a held claim means the handler is executing this instant (healthy_in_progress -- the shape a long local activity holds while scheduling no queue row at all) but ONLY while a live worker still polls its queue, since a claim left behind by a crashed worker is a poison-pill orphan (#367) and reports workflow_no_worker; a PENDING row means the decision cycle is awaiting dispatch and is classified by the same hard-impediment-first ladder an activity row uses -- workflow_queue_paused when an operator holds that queue, then workflow_no_worker (the workflow-task analogue of the no-live-worker stall) when nothing polls it, which outranks a not-yet-due dispatcher deferral on purpose because, unlike a timed sleep, a deferral only self-heals if something claims the row when the timestamp arrives, then healthy_in_progress; and a parked row (RUNNING with a NULL worker, which advances on a wake rather than a claim) is left to the lost-task verdict unchanged. A terminal execution returns health = terminal with terminal_outcome and NO blocked_on. Payload-free apart from the task row's own error text: names, ids, timestamps and queue/bucket keys only -- never an activity input, signal payload or output. That one error string IS routed through read-path payload decoding (#608), exactly as /stack routes the same column for its own last_failure, so an admin never reads plaintext there and a ciphertext envelope here. Admin-gated (the eligibility endpoints' posture: the body names queue, rate-limit and concurrency keys plus fleet coverage state). Shard-local: routed O(1) from the exec id's embedded shard, no cross-shard fan-out. An unfired durable timer more than 60s past its deadline reports timer_overdue (stalled) rather than a healthy sleep -- but ONLY when that timer actually owns the workflow's wake. Timers fire when a worker claims the owning workflow task, and only persist_started_timer reschedules that task to the deadline; every *_park path (signal wait, mutex acquire, activity wait, scheduled activities, child workflows, external handoff) discards the armed deadline and parks the task on the thing being awaited, so a timer armed alongside one of those goes overdue as a matter of course and fires on that wait's completion wake. The verdict is therefore gated on the task row itself -- a claimed or parked row means some other wake owns the run, so the more precise handoff/child/signal cause is reported instead, and only a PENDING row long past its own scheduled_at is a genuinely missed timer wake. Conversely, a durable side-table wait does not advance on its own either: a timer fires only when a worker claims the owning workflow task, so a HARD impediment on that task -- an operator queue pause (#619) or no live poller -- outranks every timer verdict and reports workflow_queue_paused / workflow_no_worker, naming the queue an operator must fix rather than a sleep that can never end. Only the hard impediments are hoisted; the task row's ordinary healthy-dispatch result stays a fallback so it never masks the more specific sleeping_timer. It is checked BELOW the activity bucket on purpose (a wedged activity names the specific thing to fix); ranking it above the handoff/child/signal categories is harmless by construction, because every one of those parks the workflow task and a parked row is not awaiting a claim. When replay diverges, the engine BLOCKS the run (#603) rather than failing it: the execution stays RUNNING and its workflow task is re-pended at a capped-exponential backoff INDEFINITELY, which by row shape alone is identical to an ordinary dispatcher deferral -- so a permanently wedged run would otherwise report healthy_in_progress. The execution row's own nd_blocked_at is authoritative and reports non_determinism_blocked (stalled) carrying the recorded divergence, the block instant and the re-fire count. It is ranked directly under paused because it is the same class of fact -- an explicit state the engine stamped on the execution row, not an inference from a liveness proxy -- and it outranks every side-table cause because the block re-fires on EVERY decision cycle regardless of what those rows are doing; nothing is lost, since a pending activity's own impediments still reach the operator through contributing_reason_codes, which is a union across rows rather than the winner's reasons. paused stays above it, mirroring the engine: a pause observed under the row lock supersedes the block and re-parks instead. Appends no WorkflowEvent, performs no task-queue mutation, adds no migration -- safe to call repeatedly.

routes.description: Reconstruct the ordered continue-as-new run chain that {id} belongs to, resolvable from ANY member (origin, a middle run, or the live/final tail). A workflow that calls continue_as_new forks forward into a fresh exec_id sharing its workflow_id and shard; over a long-lived self-continuing workflow this produces a chain of executions, and this endpoint returns all of them oldest-first as a flat list so one logical run's whole history is discoverable from a single member. The chain lives entirely on one shard (a successor inherits the predecessor's shard), so this is one shard-local gather, never a cross-shard fan-out. No new events are appended and no state is recomputed. Post-feature (issue #701) rows carry back-link columns (continued_from_exec_id, first_exec_id) so the chain resolves in one indexed query; legacy rows written before the feature carry no back-links and are gathered best-effort by forward-walking WorkflowContinuedAsNew events (bounded), with head_unknown=true when the true origin cannot be proven from the available rows. head_unknown=false for a fully post-feature chain and for a standalone never-continued run (runs has exactly one entry). Each run reports exec_id, run_id, sequence (zero-based chain ordinal), state, started_at, completed_at, outcome (collapsed terminal label), and continued_to_exec_id (the next ordered run's exec_id; null for the tail). continued_to_exec_id is derived purely from ordering so it stays correct for legacy chains that never stored a forward index. Documented graceful degradation: in a mixed chain (legacy prefix then post-feature suffix) resolved from a post-feature member, the boundary run is reported as the confirmed head and its truly-first legacy predecessors are unreachable.

routes.description: Replay ONE execution's recorded history against the currently-registered #[workflow] handler on this node and return a structured determinism verdict (issue #614). POST is used instead of GET because it drives a replay of the workflow function; this route never writes workflow events and performs no writes (read-only, admin-gated). The DB connection is dropped before user code is driven, and the replay is pure in-memory replay. Answers 'will — or did — this run diverge under the code deployed right now?': useful for a PAUSED or non-determinism-blocked RUNNING run (the divergence object mirrors the #603 block diagnostic: kind/event_index/expected/actual), or a terminal FAILED run for retroactive forensics. The verdict is one of: clean (message 'no divergence under current code'), diverged (with a divergence object), workflow_failed (with a failure object), not_registered (the workflow type is not registered on this node), or not_replayable_dag (a classic DAG is not on the replay path). Since issue #952 a terminal FAILED run whose history REPRODUCES its recorded failure under the current code is 'clean' (reproducing a recorded failure is not a divergence) and carries that error in the failure object, with message 'no divergence under current code; the recorded failure was reproduced'; 'workflow_failed' remains for a replay that failed where the recorded history did not. All five verdicts return 200 — the diagnosis, not the HTTP status, carries the answer. The replay runs in canary mode, so a healthy in-flight run parked mid-flight (a PAUSED/RUNNING frontier suspension) is correctly reported clean rather than a false diverged; a terminal run externally sealed mid-await (TIMED_OUT/cancelled/terminated) is likewise clean. The replay is bounded by WorkerConfig::query_timeout; the query_timeout bound applies to async-yielding replays, and a workflow that busy-loops synchronously without ever awaiting is out of scope, exactly as for the live executor.

routes.description: Server-Sent Events stream of the EPHEMERAL live-output progress chunks a running workflow publishes via ctx.publish_progress (issue #791). Chunks are ordered over Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY with sub-second delivery. This is a best-effort side channel: chunks are never recorded in harvest_events, never replayed, and there is NO backfill on (re)connect — a subscriber that connects after a chunk was published will not see it (chunk content may be non-deterministic precisely because it is never stored). Each SSE message carries id (a monotonic, epoch-prefixed seq — a gap means a missed chunk) plus event:progress and data (the raw chunk JSON, NOT re-wrapped). A final event:end frame is emitted when the execution reaches a terminal state and the stream then closes; event:error is sent if the LISTEN connection drops. Keepalive :ping comments keep proxies from idling the connection; the terminal-close poll cadence is a modest default bounded by the configured SSE keepalive interval. AUTH: this route inherits the management API's configured auth middleware (HarvestPlugin::api_with_auth); it is deliberately NOT admin-gated (AC5 — end-users stream their own workflows). If no api_with_auth middleware is configured the route is open — embedders exposing streams to untrusted end-users should configure api_with_auth or front it with their own auth. The engine only checks that the execution exists (else 404) — exec_id is effectively a bearer capability for this run's live chunk CONTENT, so embedders exposing sensitive output MUST add per-execution authorization. Each subscriber holds one dedicated (non-pooled) Postgres LISTEN connection for the stream's lifetime; embedders should rate-limit and/or cap concurrent streams per user to avoid DB connection exhaustion (a global concurrent-stream cap is a possible future enhancement).

params.name: id
params.description: Execution UUID.

success_response.note: Content-Type: text/event-stream. Frames: event:progress (data = the published chunk JSON, id = monotonic seq), a terminal event:end, or event:error. If the execution is already terminal at connect, a single event:end frame is sent and the stream closes. SEQ CLIENT CONTRACT: id is a monotonic per-execution LOGICAL-POSITION identity (not a per-chunk counter). Subscribers should dedupe by seq (keep-first) for at-most-once-per-position display, and use forward seq JUMPS to detect gaps after reconnect. A re-driven workflow position re-emits the SAME seq (best-effort); a re-emitted chunk MAY carry different content for non-deterministic chunks — the first-delivered is canonical. seq is per exec_id; a continue-as-new successor is a new exec_id on a new stream whose seq restarts. Chunks may be DROPPED best-effort under back-pressure (slow client) — the monotonic seq lets the client detect the resulting gap.

fields.name: conflict_policy
fields.description: How to handle a collision with a currently-ACTIVE (RUNNING/PAUSED) prior run (issue #685). Orthogonal to reuse_policy (which governs terminal priors). One of: unspecified (default — each reuse policy's native active behavior, byte-for-byte identical to today), fail (409 AlreadyExists), use_existing (return the existing run, 200, no new WorkflowStarted), terminate_existing (cancel the active prior and start fresh, 201). Sending the field (even 'unspecified') surfaces a started_fresh boolean in the response (true = fresh run created, false = attached to the existing run); omitting it keeps the response byte-for-byte identical to today. terminate_existing requires admin authentication, because it can cancel a live prior; the other values (unspecified, fail, use_existing) do not — except that unspecified inherits the reuse policy's native behavior, so reuse_policy=terminate_if_running with an omitted/unspecified conflict_policy still requires admin. Not supported combined with a throttle/debounce/batch policy — the start is deferred and has no active prior to resolve at request time (400). An unknown value returns 400. A prior sealed MIGRATED/MIGRATING by a shard rebalance (issue #964) counts as ACTIVE -- the run is live, just on another shard -- and terminate_existing against one is REFUSED with a retryable 503 naming the live residence rather than replaced: the terminate could not reach the live copy from the prior's shard, and replacing would release the business key while the real run kept executing, producing two live runs for one workflow_id. Cancel or terminate the execution by id (which routes to its live residence), then retry the start.

fields.name: idempotency_key
fields.description: Request-scoped idempotency key (issue #808). Two starts carrying the same key within the retention window (default 24h) converge on exactly one execution: the first creates it, the second returns the same execution_id as a no-op (200, no second WorkflowStarted, no second task). Dedup scope is (workflow_name, idempotency_key), independent of workflow_id, and short-circuits the reuse_policy matrix. A committed keyed replay short-circuits to the 200 no-op before fresh-start-only validations (input-schema #373, completion-callback SSRF #605, delay/start_at) and before the admission gate #377, returning the original execution regardless of the retry's body; a genuinely fresh keyed start (no live claim) still runs every validation and the gate. The `Idempotency-Key` request header takes precedence over this body field; a present-but-empty key returns 400. Mutually exclusive with a throttle/debounce/batch policy (400 if combined). Shard routing: a keyed start with an OMITTED (auto-generated) workflow_id routes by the key so same-key retries co-locate and dedup; a keyed start with an EXPLICIT workflow_id routes by workflow_id (preserving the reuse_policy matrix and the shard-local (workflow_name, workflow_id) uniqueness invariant). For dedup to converge across a delivery's retries, be consistent about supplying vs. omitting workflow_id.

fields.name: shard_id
fields.description: Pin this workflow to a concrete shard for data-residency or tenant-isolation placement (issue #697). Mutually exclusive with residency_key. Omitting both keeps today's rendezvous routing byte-for-byte. Returns 400 when the shard is outside the deployment's readable_shards, has been drained out of writable_shards, is negative, or is the reserved routing sentinel — never a silent fallback to the default shard. The pinned shard is inherited by child workflows, continue-as-new successors, workflow-level retries, and reset forks, so residency is transitive across the whole workflow tree. Consistency caveat: for a given workflow_id, pin consistently across every start — an unpinned start of the same workflow_id routes by hash to a different shard and cannot see the pinned run, so the shard-local (workflow_name, workflow_id) uniqueness invariant would not catch it. A retry of a keyed start must likewise repeat the same placement, since the placement determines which shard holds the idempotency claim.

fields.name: residency_key
fields.description: Pin this workflow via an operator-declared residency key, e.g. 'eu' (issue #697). Mutually exclusive with shard_id. Resolved through the router's declared residency map (ShardRouter::with_residency_map), which is stable across process restarts and across any widening of the readable/writable shard sets. An undeclared or blank key returns 400 rather than falling back to the rendezvous hash.

Returns 200 when conflict_policy=use_existing attaches to an ACTIVE (RUNNING/PAUSED) prior (issue #685); returns 201 when conflict_policy=terminate_existing cancels the active prior and starts fresh. When the request sends a conflict_policy field (even 'unspecified'), the response includes started_fresh (true = created a new run, false = attached to the existing run); omitting conflict_policy omits started_fresh so the response is byte-for-byte identical to today. Returns 200 with {..., started_fresh: false, deduplicated: true} when an idempotency_key (issue #808) matched an earlier same-key start (no new execution created); a fresh idempotency_key start returns 201 with {..., started_fresh: true, deduplicated: false}. The `Idempotency-Key` header may supply the key out-of-band instead of the body field. Returns 202 Accepted with {debounced, workflow_name, workflow_id, debounce_key, fire_at, pending_count} (and no execution_id) when the workflow declares a debounce policy whose key resolves (issue #499). Returns 202 Accepted with {batched, flushed, workflow_name, workflow_id, batch_key, fire_at, pending_count, max_size} when the workflow declares a batch policy. When the request supplies an explicit shard_id or residency_key (issue #697), the response echoes the resolved shard_id so an operator can audit placement without decoding the execution_id UUID; unpinned starts omit the field.

routes.description: Force-terminate a single workflow execution. The forceful sibling of cancel: seals a live run in the TERMINATED state unilaterally (no workflow-body cooperation required), fails outstanding task-queue rows, and runs the parent-close cascade. Result-awaiting callers observe a terminal failure carrying the supplied reason, distinguishable from a normal FAILED. Interrupting an already-executing hot workflow task is the domain of the workflow-task timeout (#494), not terminate.

routes.description: Re-run a terminal workflow execution: start a BRAND-NEW execution from the source run's recorded start parameters. When the re-run reuses the source's business key (the default), the source row is SEALED to CONTINUED_AS_NEW so the business key is free for the new run — its recorded prior state is returned as source_prior_state, and its output/error/completed_at are preserved untouched. Admin-only. Provenance on the new run is start_source='rerun', start_source_ref=<source execution id>, started_by=<actor>. Cloned verbatim from the source row: input (unless overridden), queue, memo, search attributes (minus the six replay-non-determinism diagnostic keys), execution timeout, chain timeout, SLA, owner/runbook_url/severity, context headers, workflow retry policy, and completion callbacks. NOT preserved: priority (it is not stored on the execution row), and schedule provenance (schedule_id / scheduled_for / origin are cleared, matching the reset-fork precedent — an operator intervention is deliberately excluded from scheduled carryover). The new run always begins a fresh continue-as-new chain and a fresh retry chain (attempt 1).
routes.idempotency: NOT idempotent. A second identical re-run returns 409: the first re-run sealed the source to CONTINUED_AS_NEW, which is no longer a re-runnable state — re-run the new run instead. (A re-run under an explicit workflow_id override does not seal the source, so the source stays re-runnable under a different key.)

params.name: id
params.description: Execution UUID of the terminal source run to re-run.

fields.name: input
fields.description: Optional replacement input for the new run. Omitted = clone the source's stored input VERBATIM — it is never decoded, so an encrypted or codec-encoded input re-runs byte-identically. A JSON null IS a valid override (it replaces the clone with null); omit the field entirely to clone. Required when the source's input has been erased (issue #495).

fields.name: workflow_id
fields.description: Optional business-key override for the new run. Omitted = reuse the source's workflow_id (which seals the source to CONTINUED_AS_NEW). When supplied and free, the new run starts under that key and the source is left untouched in its original terminal state.

success_response.notes: The response never echoes the input payload. reran_from is the source execution id; source_prior_state is the source's terminal state as observed BEFORE any sealing (e.g. "FAILED"), which is otherwise lost once the row is sealed to CONTINUED_AS_NEW.

error_responses.description: Malformed execution id or malformed JSON body; the target is a registered DAG (use the DAG trigger/retry routes); the workflow type carries a debounce, throttle, or batch policy — those defer the start and return no execution id, so a re-run cannot honour its 201 contract; an explicitly supplied `input` override violates the workflow's published input JSON Schema (issue #373), which returns the standard {error: "input validation failed", violations: [{message, field_path}]} body (only an OVERRIDE is validated: a verbatim clone of the source's stored input is never re-validated, so a run started under an older or looser schema stays re-runnable); or the source's stored `completion_callbacks` value cannot be parsed as JSON (issue #605) — a standard RFC 7807 {detail: <message>} body naming the source execution.
Execution not found, or its workflow type is no longer registered.

Source is not terminal (RUNNING/PAUSED); source is CONTINUED_AS_NEW (re-run the chain's latest run instead); source already has an automatic workflow-level retry successor (issue #523 — re-run the chain's latest attempt instead); source input has been erased (issue #495) and no explicit input was supplied; the source's shard has been drained out of writable_shards (this entire operation is pinned to the source's physical shard — a re-run can only ever land there, so an operator draining that shard blocks new re-runs of its work just like any other new admission); a workflow_id override routes to a DIFFERENT shard than the source (cross-shard workflow_id overrides are not supported — re-run without an override, or start a fresh execution directly under the target workflow_id); source is schedule-attributed and sealing it would break the schedule's carryover and run-history lineage (issues #488 / #534 — re-run with an explicit workflow_id override instead, which never seals the source); the target business key is currently held by a different live execution (including a workflow_id override that is already in use); or a stored context_headers / workflow_retry_policy value on the source cannot be parsed as JSON (a faithful clone must never silently drop a field).

The new run's input exceeds the effective workflow-input byte cap (issue #252). Fires on an oversized `input` override, and — notably — can also fire on the VERBATIM CLONE of a source that started successfully under a larger cap, if an operator has since LOWERED `max_workflow_input_bytes` (globally or for this workflow type). In that case the source is re-runnable only by supplying a smaller `input` override or by raising the cap back.

A completion callback target CLONED VERBATIM from the source (issue #605) is no longer admissible under the live SSRF policy — e.g. it was valid when the source started but has since been dropped from the host allowlist. Body: {error: "completion callback target rejected", url, rejection}, where `rejection` is a machine-readable SsrfRejection object (tag: `code`, e.g. HostNotAllowlisted/SchemeNotAllowed/IpLiteralNotAllowed). Only fires when the source has `completion_callbacks` recorded; a source with none is unaffected. Nothing is started and the source is never sealed.
An admission gate blocked the new start — same body shape as any gated start (error, gate_id, reason).

routes.description: Tombstone all payload-bearing fields (input, output, payload, details, value, last_completion_result) in every event row, the execution row, and signal rows for a terminal workflow execution. Cascades to terminal child executions on the same shard. Requires the execution to be in a terminal state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMED_OUT, CONTINUED_AS_NEW, or TERMINATED). Scrubs EVERY shard that still holds a copy of the execution: a shard rebalance (issue #964) seals rather than deletes the source, so a rebalanced run's payloads live on both the live target and the sealed source until the source shard's retention collects it, and each additional residence that was scrubbed is reported in the response's prior_residences array. The terminal-state and legal-hold gates are evaluated against the LIVE residence only, so a still-running execution can never be erased through its own sealed shadow. A residence whose copy has already been collected contributes nothing and is not an error; a residence this node cannot reach fails the whole call, because an erasure that cannot be shown to be complete must not be reported as complete. The one exception is a RETIRED shard -- decommissioned, its pool removed fleet-wide and its ids forwarded to a successor per docs/runbooks/shard-decommission.md, which requires its payloads to be destroyed or erased before the forward is declared. Those are listed in retired_residences rather than failing the call, since failing closed on them would make every run that ever lived on a retired shard permanently un-erasable.

routes.description: Force-fail exactly one hung in-flight (RUNNING) activity task. Appends ActivityFailed with the distinct error_type 'OperatorForceFailed' through the existing recording path (no new event variant), marks the task row FAILED with the typed failure envelope, and wakes the parked workflow task so the owning workflow advances to its own failure/compensation path -- it is NOT terminated. Note: if the owning workflow has a workflow-level retry policy (issue #523) and propagates this error to workflow failure, the run is retried fresh and the activity re-dispatched -- use cancel/terminate instead if the goal is to stop the run. routes.idempotency: Idempotent: re-issuing the call on an already-forced task (FAILED with the OperatorForceFailed envelope) is a no-op success returning forced=false, already_forced=true, with zero writes and no second terminal event. Idempotency wins over the terminal-execution guard: a retry issued after the woken workflow has consumed the forced failure and sealed its own run (the expected aftermath of a successful force-fail) still returns the no-op success rather than the terminal 409.

GET /admin/start-throttle only surfaces override state for a workflow while it has pending backlog rows; this route answers reliably even when the backlog has fully drained but the override is still running for the rest of its TTL, or before any pressure has occurred at all. Buckets are shard-local (issue #607/#247); the top-level 200/207 body reports whichever reachable shard has a LIVE override whenever any shard does -- never the mere fewest-remaining-tokens row, since raw token count says nothing about whether an operator override is active (issue #945 review, round 4, P2). routes.description: Report payload-codec key rotation progress per shard (issue #948). Lists every registered codec key id, which one is active for new writes, and -- per shard -- how many harvest_events rows still carry each key id plus the lazy re-encryption sweep's durable resume cursor. This is the screen an operator watches to know when an outgoing key has zero remaining rows. A zero census is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for retirement: it proves no row references the key right now on the shards this process can reach, not that no worker is still encoding under it and no already-encoded append is still in flight. Retirement additionally requires an attested fleet write fence -- see the procedure in docs/operations/codec-key-rotation.md. Treating zero here as authorization to destroy key material can leave a late-committing row permanently unreadable. An unreachable shard degrades the response to `status: "partial"` and is named in `unavailable_shards`; `rows_remaining_total` is then a LOWER BOUND, not a count -- an unread shard's rows are unknown, never zero. The retirement gate applies the same fail-closed rule and refuses to retire a key while any expected shard is unreadable. On a deployment with no keyed codecs registered -- every deployment that has not adopted key rotation -- `registered_key_ids` is empty, `active_key_id` is the legacy sentinel, and every count is zero.

success_response.notes: `sink_configured` reports ONLY whether the process serving this request has an audit sink installed. It is not a fleet-wide signal and must not be diagnosed from: in a split web/worker deployment an API process legitimately reports false while export is healthy on the worker fleet, and true would not establish that the process actually running the scanner is configured. The database-backed signals -- `pending_records` growing across two reads, `lag_seconds` rising, or a persistent NOT_STARTED -- describe the shard rather than whichever process answered. RETIRED means an operator ran decommission_cursor: the cursor row survives only to preserve the sequence high-water mark, no exporter owes the shard records, and retention may purge them, so the entry's other fields are a frozen snapshot rather than live state. routes.description: Rewind one shard's audit-export cursor so already-delivered audit records are re-exported to the SIEM sink (issue #953), for recovery after sink-side data loss. Re-exported records are byte-identical -- the per-record export sequence is never re-stamped, so a record carries the same (shard, seq) and the same JSON on every delivery and the receiver dedupes on that pair. A cursor may only ever move BACKWARDS: a request that would move it forward, or leave it where it is, is refused with 400 rather than applied, because advancing it would mark records delivered that never were. The `before` form resolves to one below the LOWEST sequence assigned to a record at or after that instant, so any clock/commit-order skew makes the rewind reach further back (costing duplicate deliveries the receiver dedupes) rather than skipping records. The redrive itself writes an audit record (`audit_export.redrive`) in the same transaction as the rewind, so re-exporting is as auditable as the operations being exported.
routes.idempotency: Idempotent in effect: the cursor ends up at the requested position. A repeat of the same request is refused with 400 rather than applied a second time, because a request that would not move the cursor BACKWARDS (at or above the current position) is never applied. Each accepted call writes its own audit record.

fields.name: to_seq
fields.description: Rewind to this exact export sequence; records with seq > to_seq re-export. Exactly one of to_seq or before must be supplied. A negative value is clamped to 0 (re-export everything still retained).

fields.name: before
fields.description: RFC 3339 instant; rewind so every audit record that occurred at or after it re-exports. Exactly one of to_seq or before must be supplied.

success_response.notes: `outcome` is `rewound`. `from` is where the cursor was, `to` where it now is; records with seq > to will be re-delivered by the exporter on its next tick. The rewind also bumps the shard's claim epoch and clears its lease, so a delivery already in flight when the rewind lands cannot acknowledge over it and silently undo the redrive. The rewind and the `audit_export.redrive` audit record are one transaction on one connection, so an applied-but-unaudited redrive is not representable; that audit row lands in the TARGET shard's audit log (not the default shard's, unlike other audited routes) because it describes a shard-scoped mutation and a second connection could neither be atomic with the rewind nor safely acquired while holding it. and the audit row's target_id records the shard AND the requested position (`shard=0;to_seq=42`), since a redrive is the one operation here that can trigger a mass re-export.

The retirement and its audit record (`audit_export.decommission`) are one transaction on one connection, on the target shard's own connection, exactly like the redrive route. A shard already retired, or never configured, changes nothing but is still audited: an auditor needs the record of the request, not only of requests that had an effect.

routes.description: Partially update an existing workflow schedule in place (issue #771). Only provided fields change; the schedule_id is never changed, so #488 carryover lineage, the sched:{schedule_id}: workflow-id namespace, and run history are preserved. The workflow type is NOT editable (400). DAG schedules are owned by PATCH /dags/{dag_name} (400). Nullable fields (calendar, consecutive_failure_limit, end_at, max_runs, catchup_policy, retry_policy) are tri-state: omitting the field leaves it unchanged, an explicit JSON null clears it. The merged spec is validated before any write, so a 400 writes nothing. Changing the schedule expression recomputes next_run_at anchored at now (elapsed slots are never retroactively fired); other edits preserve the pending next_run_at. Anti-race with the scheduler tick: an edit is rejected 409 while a fire claim is live, an expired claim is fenced (token nulled) so a straggler fire cannot finalize over the edit, and a tick that wins its claim re-reads the row before firing, so a fire that lands concurrently with the edit always dispatches the committed new input/queue/policies.
routes.idempotency: Idempotent for identical bodies: re-applying the same partial update converges on the same row state. Returns 409 while a scheduler replica holds a live fire claim on the row (the claim lease is bounded at ~30 s); retry shortly.
